ELI5: What are the differences between a CEO, the owner, and the manager of a company?

The owner literally owns the company, the CEO runs the company but not necessarily owns it, and a manager runs a specific part of the company (A.K.A. department).

As a bonus: a supervisor gives directions to employees in a given department, but doesn't truly run that department. A lead also gives direction, but doesn't really have disciplinary authority. And an asshole is someone who is none of those things, but acts like they are anyway.

It depends on the type of company. For example, in a smaller, privately owned company, the owner is often the CEO and hence, the manager of the company. In a corporation it's more complicated. These types of companies are owned by a multitude of stockholders. Sometimes a few, other times millions of them. That's why the board (which consists of the major stockholders who vote on important decisions concerning management) assign the role of CEO to a specific person. Usually a member of the board but it's not necessary. This person is charged with running the company and is liable of both successful and failed operations. Hope you find this reply helpful :)

Think of it like this, you buy a ball. You now own the ball. However, you want to make the ball better. You have two options, you can try to make it better yourself, or you can pay someone else to do what they can to make it better. That would be the CEO. An owner of a company can be the CEO but he/she does not have to be. The CEO could just be an exemplary employee who you trust to run the company. Now sometimes there can be multiple owners of a company, this happens a lot with bigger companies, and this group of people is called the Board of Directors. All of the BOD hold major portions of shares of the company. However, the one with the grand majority shares is usually the only one referred to as "owning" the company. As for managers, the CEO is technically the main manager of the company so those are practically one in the same. Hope this helps.

As you may know, everything in Swift is by default "internal" rather than "private". This means you have to make things public if you want to write unit tests. Swift 2.0 introduces the @testable annotation which gives you access to "internal" stuff from outside of your project. Cool.

My company is developing an app and the management is starting to require code to have at least some unit tests. I've talked with my boss and he understands the issues with Swift 1.2 unit testing and agrees that we could just wait until xCode 7 is out of beta (in the fall. hopefully?) and then convert our project to 2.0 and begin writing unit tests.

My question is, is that the right way to go about this? Our app isn't going to be huge. Converting to 2.0 shouldn't be too bad. What can I test now, with Swift 1.2, without making all my view controllers and models public?

Thanks.
Waiting until Swift 2.0 to write unit tests.

Try to do your tests from the behavioral level. Another thing you can consider is using the Xcode 7 features that allow you to record tests by interacting with the screen--then, you could run Xcode-7 somewhere so that it could do your behavioral tests, and then you could do your main development in Xcode 6.

Swift 2.0 looks pretty damn sweet. The toolchain is stable at this point, and they're doing their work on the development tools--like the highlighting engine, IDE, and whatnot. We're considering taking some stuff to production in it here in a month or two at my company.
